paper_title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Photos from modern cameras have tens of megapixels (MP), but the detail that answers question about them is often only few dozen pixels wide, such as what pedestrian down the street is holding. Such photos exceed the input size of vision-language models. For example, Qwen3.5 turns each patch of 32 32 pixels into one token, so 45 MP photo would require about 44,000 tokens. Models therefore cap the input size, even with high-resolution encoders [3, 22, 39, 61], and shrink larger photos to fit. The detail shrinks with the photo and often becomes unreadable [66, 73, 84]. At the 3.8 MP limit of Claude Haiku 5.5, detail 50 pixels wide in 45 MP photo becomes about 15 pixels wide. To recover such details, visual agents view the whole photo at low resolution and zoom into the regions they need [50, 60]. Some follow fixed search procedure [35, 40, 41, 57, 67, 82], and others learn where to zoom [13, 25, 33, 53, 59, 83, 85, 87]. Correct without reading. However, correct answer does not show that the agent read the evidence, because common sense often gives the same answer [1, 19, 38, 49, 64, 75]. For example, person who holds up small device as if taking photo usually holds smartphone. An agent can therefore answer smartphone correctly without reading the device. Figure 1a tests this with three versions of 45 MP street photo, in which woman holds up smartphone, calculator or TV remote. The device fits in square of 110 pixels, so model must zoom in to read it. Without zoom tool, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna answer smartphone for all three versions. The released agents DeepEyes [87] and ZoomEye [57] give the same answer, although they can zoom. Even with zoom tool and its highest thinking level, Claude Haiku 5.5 still identifies the remote as smartphone. Being able to zoom therefore does not make an agent read the evidence. Existing methods. The agents that learn where to zoom are trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer [21, 29], typically with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [55]. This training cannot correct the guess, because on single image, guess earns the same reward as reading. The guess is also easier, because it requires no zoom, so it becomes shortcut that the reward cannot detect [10, 16, 77, 79]. Recent work therefore also rewards the zoom, such as tool call [87], crop that covers annotated evidence [11, 86] or call that improves the answer [14, 51]. These rewards credit viewing the evidence rather than reading it, and agents learn to call the zoom tool without using what it shows [25, 47, 69, 90]. For example, on the TV remote version of Figure 1a, DeepEyes zooms onto the whole remote but writes that the zoomed-in image confirms that the person is holding smartphone. Given only this zoom in new conversation, it answers TV remote. Other methods mask the evidence and reward abstention or penalize an answer [42, 74]. However, masked image has no answer to read, so they cannot check whether the answer changes with the evidence. Both still judge one image at time. Contrast sets. On one image, reading and guessing give the same answer, so no reward on that image can separate them. Several versions of the same photo can. contrast set [15] asks the same question about several versions of photo. Only small region with the evidence differs between them, so the versions have different answers, as in Figure 1a. An agent that gives the same answer to every version can be correct on only one of them, so only reading the evidence can solve the whole set. We call the share of sets that an agent solves its set accuracy. Contrast sets and similar minimal pairs have been used to evaluate vision-language models [17, 34, 63] and to train them with supervised losses [7, 31, 62]. We build such sets for zoom agents by editing one small object in real photos of 21 to 120 MP. ViRA-Train has 9,261 sets with 𝐾 = 1, 2 or 3 versions for training, 2 Figure 2. Examples of ViRA-Bench and ViRA-Bench-Real. Each set shows the original photo (O, cut to 16:9) with the object in yellow box. The insets show the object in and the two variants (A, B), with the correct answers. Below each set are the originals answer and the number of baseline settings, out of 15 (Appendix D.1), that give this answer to all three versions at 1 MP. Questions are shortened. and ViRA-Bench has 762 sets for evaluation. In ViRA-Bench, the edited object covers median of 0.0075% of the photo. We also photograph 78 sets in which only the real object changes between shots (ViRA-Bench-Real), so they involve no editing. Figure 2 shows examples of both benchmarks, on which many of the models we test give the same answer to all three versions. CrossRPO. GRPO samples several answers (rollouts) for one input and compares them with each other (Figure 3, top). If it trains on each version of contrast set separately, no reward depends on solving the whole set. If it compares rollouts across versions (pooled GRPO), guess that is correct on one version scores above the wrong answers on the others and is rewarded. We therefore propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO, Figure 3, bottom). It compares each rollout only with rollouts of the same version, so guess that is always correct on one version receives no credit. It then scales the result with cross-input weight. The weight grows when the other versions are answered correctly, because correct answer on this version then solves the set. CrossRPO applies to sets of any size, including single images, whereas recent methods for two inputs [12, 27, 37, 89, 91] handle only pairs. We prove that its update is unbiased and does not reinforce set answered from common sense, and that the objectives of GRPO and of these two-input methods are special cases of its objective. ViRA. With CrossRPO, we train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, on about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. With the same data and reward, CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO on each version separately and 52.6% for pooled GRPO. Training on each version separately, without the cross-input weight, achieves 58.7%. CrossRPO loses its gain over separate training when the cross-input weight comes from photos of other questions, so the gain depends on the contrast sets. ViRA-9B zooms onto the object as often as the agent trained on each version separately, but it reads the object correctly more 3 often. ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B are the most accurate open agents of their sizes on ten and nine of the ten benchmarks we test, respectively. On ViRA-Bench, ViRA-27B also outperforms all proprietary models we test at every resolution (Figure 1b). Contributions. Our contributions are as follows. We propose CrossRPO, which trains on sets of inputs of any size. We prove that its update is unbiased, that it does not reinforce set answered from common sense, and that the objectives of GRPO and of recent two-input methods are special cases of its objective. We build ViRA-Train and ViRA-Bench, contrast sets made by editing one small object in photos of 21 to 120 MP, and ViRA-Bench-Real, photographed sets in which only the real object changes. We train ViRA-9B and 27B with CrossRPO. Our experiments show that ViRA models outperform the models with similar size on most benchmarks. We will release all data, code and models.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Zooming agents. Thinking-with-images agents [50, 60] crop and zoom over several turns. They are trained with supervised data [53] or with RL on the final answer [13, 25, 33, 59, 83, 85, 87]. Other methods search the image without training [35, 57, 67, 82] or learn to see fine details without zooming [70, 81]. Recent rewards credit crops that cover the evidence [11, 86] or calls that outperform random crop or no call [14, 51], but they still judge one image at time. Audits find that the returned crops often matter little [54, 69, 90] and that the gains come mostly from the model [47]. Except for PerceptRL [20], these works compare with proprietary models that view the image once and have no zoom tool [51, 59, 70, 71, 81], whereas we give them our zoom tool at their highest thinking level. Learning from contrasts. Contrast sets and similar minimal pairs [15, 17, 34, 63] test whether answers follow the image, and they credit model only if it answers every member correctly. Counterfactual examples also serve as supervised training data [7, 31, 62]. For RL, reward on the final answer cannot distinguish an answer that is read from the image from an answer that is based on priors [42, 77, 79]. DeFacto [74] and EVAN [42] therefore add training signals from inputs without the evidence, whereas our versions replace the evidence, so every version has an answer to read. GRPO [21, 55] and its variants [2, 44, 80, 88] compare rollouts of one prompt, also for vision-language models [26, 45, 56, 68]. Recent methods train on augmented or rephrased copies of an input with the same answer [43, 76, 89, 91], on counterfactual pairs [12, 27, 37] or on packs of inputs [28, 30]. CRPO [12] weights an input and its transformed copy by the accuracy on the other, and CrossRPO extends this coupling to any number of inputs (Appendix A.11).

sections.content: On single image, correct guess earns the same reward as reading, so RL on final answers cannot distinguish them. contrast set can distinguish them, because guess is correct on only one of its versions. CrossRPO turns this difference into training signal for visual agents. Figure 3 compares its pipeline with GRPO. The theorems, propositions and their proofs are in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4 ViRA-Bench and ViRA-Train
sections.content: CrossRPO requires sets whose versions differ only in the evidence and have different correct answers. This section introduces three datasets of such sets, ViRA-Bench, ViRA-Bench-Real and ViRA-Train, which are built from ultra-high-resolution photos of 21 MP to 120 MP. Building contrast set. The original photos are color photos from Wikimedia Commons. We use vision-language model to find an object in photo that can be changed into 𝐾 1 other versions. For 𝐾 = 3, smartphone in hand (the original 𝑠1) can be changed into calculator (variant 𝑠2) and TV remote (variant 𝑠3), as in Figure 1a. An image editor redraws the object for each variant, and 7 only the region of the old and new object is pasted back into the photo. language model writes question 𝑞 about the object with four options, including the correct answer 𝑦𝑣 of every version and at least one distractor. The question first states the location of the object and never names the changed attribute. Some variants contradict common sense, so model that guesses gives the originals answer (Figure 2). The same versions can serve several sets: another question 𝑞 with answers 𝑦 𝑣 gives the set (𝑞, (𝑠𝑣, 𝑦 ). After automatic checks, human reviewers check every ViRA-Bench question (Appendix B.1). 𝑣) 𝐾 𝑣= ViRA-Bench contains 762 contrast sets on 466 photos of 24 to 108 MP (Figure 2). Each set has 𝐾 = 3 versions, the original and the two variants and B. An object is kept only if its longer side is at most 13 pixels when the photo is reduced to 1 MP and its shorter side is at least 28 pixels at full resolution, so model must zoom in to read it. The edited object covers median of 0.0075% of the photo (Figure 4b). Of the questions, 458 ask for visible property, 209 add step of reasoning, and 95 involve several objects. The metric is set accuracy, the share of sets with all three versions answered correctly. The first zoom of every agent covers the object equally often on the edited variants and on the original (Appendix B.2): the two shares differ by at most 2.4 percentage points at every budget. Figure 4. Statistics of ViRA-Bench and ViRA-BenchReal. (a) Size of the 466 ViRA-Bench photos, and every ViRA-Bench-Real photo has 45.4 MP. (b) Cumulative distribution of the objects area as share of the photo, with dots at the medians. ViRA-Bench-Real. To exclude editing traces, ViRA-Bench-Real contains 78 sets that were photographed without any editing (Figure 2, right; Appendix B.3). Its 234 photos were taken with Nikon Z8 camera. Between the three shots of set, only the object was swapped. The swapped objects are posters, signs, stickers, labels and small everyday objects. The photos have 45.4 MP, and the objects cover median of 0.0017% of the photo. ViRA-Train contains 6,457 contrast sets on 3,797 Commons photos of 21 to 120 MP that are not in ViRA-Bench (Appendix B.4). Of these sets, 4,110 have three versions and 2,347 have two. The edited region has shorter side of at least 20 pixels at full resolution, and its longer side has median of 16 pixels at 1 MP. ViRA-Train also contains 2,804 single images as sets with 𝐾 = 1. They are questions about details in Commons photos, questions about several objects in photos and maps, math problems from ThinkLite-VL [68] and synthetic charts.

sections.title: 5.2 Main results
sections.content: Table 1 gives the set accuracy and the tokens per set of every model on ViRA-Bench and ViRA-BenchReal, and Table 2 gives the accuracy of every model on the general benchmarks. Both tables group the models into the 79B models, the 2732B models and the proprietary models, and Δ row gives the gain of ViRA over its base model with the zoom tool. ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B are the most accurate open models of their sizes on ten and nine of the ten benchmarks. ViRA-Bench. Without zoom tool, no open model solves more than 15.1% of the sets below its maximum resolution  (Table 1)  . The gain of ViRA-9B over its base model with the zoom tool grows 11 with the budget, from 17.6 to 28.7 points. The released 79B agents stay below the untrained Qwen3.5-9B with the zoom tool at every budget: they reach per-image accuracy of 30 to 51%  (Table 16)  but solve at most 21.1% of the sets. ViRA-9B is also ahead of the open 27B models with the zoom tool, and ViRA-27B, after RL on only 3,401 items, is ahead of every proprietary model at every budget. Claude Haiku 5.5 at max thinking uses about 2 to 6 times as many tokens as ViRA-9B (Figure 1b) and is ahead of it below the maximum resolution. Both proprietary models are less accurate at every budget with medium thinking and again without thinking, and GPT-6-Luna at max thinking falls from 55.6% at 4 MP to 26.6% at its maximum resolution. Figure 5 shows where nine agents look on one contrast set. ViRA-Bench-Real. ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B also lead the open models of their sizes on photographed sets  (Table 1)  , so their lead does not depend on edited images. Without zoom tool, no open model solves more than 5.1% of the sets below its maximum resolution. The released 79B agents reach per-image accuracy of 30 to 60%  (Table 16)  but solve at most 28.2% of the sets. ViRA-27B is within 0.5 points of Claude Haiku 5.5 at 0.5 MP and ahead of it from 1 MP on. General benchmarks. ViRA-9B gains 5.6 to 21.8 points over its base model with the zoom tool, and ViRA-27B gains 3.5 to 24.4 points  (Table 2)  . Among the open models of their sizes, ViRA-9B is the most accurate on all eight benchmarks and ViRA-27B on seven. ZoomEye searches tree of crops with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and is not trained. On and HR-Bench, its accuracy is within the range of the five trained agents, but it is 9.8 to 19.9 points below ViRA-9B. ViRA-27B is ahead of both proprietary models on five of the eight benchmarks.

sections.title: 5.3 Ablations
sections.content: All ablations  (Table 3)  start from Qwen3.5-9B with the same data, reward, protocol and number of steps as ViRA-9B, and only the advantage changes (Appendix G.1). Joint term. Without the joint term (𝜆 = 0), each version is trained separately with RLOO, and set accuracy on ViRA-Bench drops at every budget, by 4.6 to 7.4 points. On the general benchmarks, accuracy changes by at most 2 points, except on O3-Bench, where it drops by 6.9 points at 1 MP. Without the joint term, the last zoom covers the object as often, but accuracy at 1 MP is 2.4 points lower on the originals and 5.2 and 5.3 points lower on the variants (Appendix H), so the joint term improves reading, not finding. Random partners. The versions in batch are assigned to the sets at random, so the weight 𝑤𝑣 of an image is computed from images of other questions. Set accuracy then stays close to that of 𝜆 = 0, as Proposition A.38 predicts. Value of 𝜆. With 𝜆 = 2, set accuracy is higher at low budgets but lower at the maximum resolution and on every general benchmark, and 𝜆 = 1 is lower on ViRA-Bench at every budget. From 2 MP on, 𝜆 = 0.5 is the most accurate variant on ViRA-Bench. With 𝜆 = 2, the agent also zooms 2.7 times per image and uses 34K to 346K tokens per set, against 12K to 147K  (Table 17)  . One group per version. Per-version GRPO is 𝜆 = 0 with the advantages of each version divided by their standard deviation. It is behind CrossRPO from 2 MP on ViRA-Bench and on every general benchmark, but ahead at 0.5 and 1 MP on ViRA-Bench and up to 4 MP on ViRA-Bench-Real. Its agent zooms two to three times per image where CrossRPO zooms once, and uses about twice as many tokens (Appendix G.2). One group per set. Pooled RLOO is 𝜆 = 0 with the leave-one-out mean taken over all rollouts of the set. On ViRA-Bench, pooled GRPO and pooled RLOO are behind CrossRPO at every budget. On ViRA-Bench-Real, both are ahead up to 2 MP, and pooled RLOO is ahead because it draws smaller zoom boxes (Appendix G.2). ConsistRoll [91], pooled GRPO with pair bonus, is behind on both benchmarks at every budget.

sections.title: 5.4 Generalizability and Scalability
sections.content: Generalization to text. The joint term does not depend on images. It needs only sets of inputs that share one question and have different answers. Questions about passages that contradict known facts give such sets in text. There, the models memory plays the role of common sense, and the passage plays the role of the evidence. We therefore train Qwen3.5-9B on text contrast sets, without images and without the zoom tool. Data. ConFiQA [4] asks questions about facts from Wikidata, and its passages were written by an LLM from these facts. We use its three subsets, which have single-hop questions (QA), multi-hop questions (MR) and multi-hop questions with several replaced facts (MC). Each ConFiQA item has the original passage and copy in which the answer entity is replaced. set with 𝐾 = 3 has the original passage (O), this copy (A) and one more copy (B), in which we replace the answer of with another entity of the same Wikidata relation. No substituted passage mentions the original answer, so an answer from the models memory is correct only on O. We hold out 1,660 questions of the three subsets for testing. Of the other questions, we train only on the 2,856 that the base model answers correctly without the passage, so its memory gives the original answer on every version. The 493 test questions with this property form the strong-prior subset in Table 4. Training. The model reads the passage and the question, reasons, and then answers with word or phrase in single turn. The reward is accuracy. An answer is correct if it contains the answer of its version or an alias, and it is wrong if it also names the answer of another version. Each step samples 16 sets, and each version has four rollouts, so set receives 12 rollouts as in the image runs. CrossRPO uses 𝜆 = 0.5, and 𝜆 = 0, pooled GRPO and pooled RLOO are defined as in Appendix G.1. All runs use the same data and 178 steps, which is about one pass over the training questions. We train each method three times with different random seeds. Test sets. The ConFiQA test questions come from the same source as the training questions. NQSwap [46] and FaithEval [48] come from other sources, and we did not train on them. NQ-Swap takes questions and Wikipedia passages from Natural Questions and replaces the answer entity in the passage. We test 1,000 random NQ-Swap questions, each with the substituted and the original passage. FaithEval (counterfactual task) has 1,000 multiple-choice science questions from ARCChallenge. For each question, an LLM wrote passage that supports counterfactual answer, and this answer is the correct option. The model answers with the letter of an option. ConFiQA and NQ-Swap answers are scored with the rule of the reward. Results. The training sets have 2,645 strong-prior questions for 𝐾 = 4 and 8 and 2,627 for 𝐾 = 16. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Visual agents often answer from common sense. In this paper, we propose CrossRPO, which trains visual agents on contrast sets, rewards solving the whole set, and provably does not reinforce set answered from common sense. We build ViRA-Train and ViRA-Bench by editing one small object in photos of 21 to 120 MP, and photograph ViRA-Bench-Real. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. After RL on about 3,500 items each, ViRA-9B leads open models of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna at their highest thinking level on most benchmarks.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Data. ViRA-Bench and ViRA-Train are made by image editing, so traces inside an edited object could affect the answer. The first zoom covers the object equally often on the edited and the unedited versions (Appendix B.2), so the edits do not guide the search, but the test does not cover reading. ViRA-Bench-Real has no edits, but it has only 78 sets, which were shot indoors with one camera and show mostly posters, signs, stickers and labels. photographed benchmark at the scale of ViRA-Bench, with outdoor scenes and more kinds of objects, would be stronger test. Each question also describes where the object is, which makes the search easier than question without this description would. The image sets have at most three versions, so larger sets are tested only on text. Method. CrossRPO requires sets whose versions differ only in the evidence and have different answers (Proposition A.40). Such sets need an image editor or second photo of the scene, so they cost more to build than single images. Its gain over 𝜆 = 0 is mainly on contrast sets. single image has no other version, so its cross-input weight is zero, and CrossRPO then trains it as RLOO does. Agents. The reward is accuracy only, so nothing encourages tight boxes or further zooms. ViRA-9B usually zooms once with large box (Appendix G.2). At low budgets, very small object then stays small in the crop, and reward on the objects size in the last view could lead to tighter boxes. Evaluation. Only one family of base models is trained. ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B start from Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B, and we have not tested CrossRPO on other architectures. The baselines run with their own tools and prompts, and the proprietary models use our tool through their APIs. The ablations of Table 3 share the data, the reward and the tool, so they isolate the effect of the advantage. Text. The text experiments are small. They train one base model for one pass over fewer than 3,000 questions of one dataset. They show that the joint term transfers to text, not the accuracy that it can reach there. We leave text experiments at larger scale to future work.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: LLMs and image editing models are part of our data pipeline and training. Appendices B.1, B.4 and C.4 name each model and its role in our pipeline. Human reviewers check every ViRA-Bench question. For ViRA-Bench-Real, Claude Code (Anthropic) proposed and designed the scenes and changes, and humans selected the proposals, took the photos, and verified and reviewed every set. Claude Code and Codex (OpenAI) also assisted with the prototype, the implementation and the writing of this paper. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted work and take full responsibility for the code, data, claims, contributions, results and text.

sections.title: A Theory of CrossRPO
sections.content: This section derives CrossRPO from first principles and proves every statement. The argument has four steps. (i) We formalize policies, sets of inputs and rollout sampling (Appendix A.1) and prove the score-function identities behind group-based policy gradients (Appendix A.2). (ii) We show that accuracy on each version cannot distinguish an answer that is read from the evidence from an answer that is taken from the prior, whereas the accuracy on whole set can. We define the objective accordingly (Appendix A.3). (iii) For an arbitrary set-level reward, we construct family of unbiased gradient estimators. The CrossRPO advantage is its closed form for our objective (Appendix A.4). (iv) The estimator involves three design choices, and prior work makes different ones. We compare them under four requirements: unbiasedness (Appendix A.5), variance (Appendix A.6), credit assignment (Appendix A.7) and scale (Appendix A.8). sections.content: This section describes ViRA-Bench (Appendix B.1) and tests whether its edits leave traces that guide the agents (Appendix B.2). It then describes ViRA-Bench-Real (Appendix B.3) and the training data (Appendix B.4). B.1 ViRA-Bench Photos. The photos come from Wikimedia Commons and have at least 24 MP, long side of at most 14,000 px and an aspect ratio between 1.2 and 2.4. All photos are in color. All licenses allow modification (CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC0 or public domain), and every photo keeps its source page, author and license so that the release can credit each image. Objects. vision-language model proposes objects whose appearance could plausibly be different, such as sign, light, small device or part of vehicle. SAM 3 [6] then segments them at full resolution. Every object has longer side of at most 13 px at 1 MP and shorter side of at least 28 px in the photo, so it can be read after zooming but not without zooming. It is whole physical object or printed design such as pictogram, and not text, face, reflection, shadow or one of mass of similar things such as leaves. Other objects of the same kind may appear if the question singles out the target. 45 Questions and edits. For each object, language model writes question and an edit instruction for each of two variants (A, B). The question has four options, which are the answers for the original (O), and and distractor. The answers of the three versions are pairwise different, so set tests whether the agents answer changes with the object. The four options belong to one category, such as arrows that point up, up-left and up-right. Changes of symbol, shape, direction and state are preferred over color, because models tend to assume the usual look of an object without looking closely. The question first locates the object and only then asks about it. It usually names large part of the photo first and then the item that carries the object, and it names neither the answer nor property that reveals it. Its answer requires no reading of text, and any reasoning uses only common knowledge. Besides questions about the object itself, some questions add one step of common-sense reasoning, such as what sign allows, and some compare the object with an unedited object elsewhere in the photo. Before editing, the plan is checked on the original, so that the answer for is correct. An image editing model then edits an enlarged crop around the object according to each instruction. The edited crop is registered to the original, and the change is restricted to the object mask. The result is then pasted back into the full-resolution photo, so the versions differ only in the region of the old and the new object. For 108 sets, both variants are chosen to contradict common sense or another cue in the photo, so guess gives the originals answer. Table 10 names the models of each step. Several models propose the objects and write the questions, so that the preferences of one model do not run through all sets. Table 10. These checks only flag candidates. Human reviewers then check every question against the three versions and the object at full resolution. They accept, correct or rewrite each question. Statistics. If editing left traces that showed an agent where to look, its first zoom would cover the object more often on and than on the unedited O. The three photos of set show the same scene, and only the object differs between them, while the camera, the light and everything else stay in place. The objects are printed posters and signs, stickers, labels and small everyday objects, and some variants contradict common sense. The photos were taken in classrooms, laboratories, library and atriums of university buildings, with Nikon Z8 camera (82565504 px) 47 and NIKKOR 14-24mm f/2.8 lens on tripod. All photos use manual exposure at ISO 64 without flash, focal lengths of 14 to 24 mm and apertures of f/2.8 to f/6.3, and the three photos of set share all settings. The questions are written from the photos and reviewed by humans, and the photos carry no metadata. B.4 ViRA-Train and the training data ViRA-Train. Of its 6,457 contrast sets, 5,329 concern text, such as the words on sign or label, and 1,128 concern objects. For text set, we detect the text in the photo, and Qwen2.5-VL-72B writes question and alternative words. Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 then replaces the words in the variants, and the result must pass an OCR check, check by Qwen2.5-VL-72B and review by Claude. Of the text questions, 2,347 ask for reasoning about the words, for example what sign allows. Claude Sonnet 5.5 writes these questions, and they have answers for and only. Of the object questions, 347 come from sets built like ViRA-Bench with Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.4 Image 2  (Table 10)  . For the other 781, Qwen2.5-VL-72B finds small objects, proposes their changes and writes the questions. Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 then edits the objects, and Claude Opus 5.5 checks the result. No ViRA-Train photo is ViRA-Bench photo or near-duplicate of one, such as photo of the same series or visually similar photo by the same author. ViRA-Train contains no contrast set that Qwen3.5-9B or Qwen2.5-VL-7B answers correctly on every version at 1 MP without tool and with greedy decoding, since such sets give no learning signal. Training data. Table 13 lists the training data of ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B. For ViRA-9B, the contrast sets are the 1,664 sets of ViRA-Train that Qwen3.5-9B does not answer entirely correctly when it views the photo at 12.8 MP without the tool. The single images serve two purposes: they keep the agents skills on ordinary questions, and they show that CrossRPO can train on sets and single images in one batch. The open questions about Commons photos were written by Claude Opus 5.5 for the six regions of 2 3 grid on each photo and checked by Gemini 3.7 Flash. For the multi-evidence questions, Gemini 3.7 Flash lists the objects in each region, and Claude Opus 5.5 writes questions of six types (position, chained reference, order, counting, attribute or absence, and reading combined with reasoning). program computes the options of the closed types from the object boxes, so that their wording cannot reveal the answer. Gemini then checks that every object named in question occurs exactly once in the photo. Every single image is neither too easy nor unsolvable for the base model, which answers it correctly in at least one and at most six of eight attempts. The training data of ViRA-27B are built from the same sources with the same rules applied to Qwen3.8-27B, which gives 1,338 contrast sets and 2,063 single images. Table 13. sections.title: D Baselines and benchmarks
sections.content: This appendix describes the 15 baselines and the benchmarks of Section 5. D.1 Baselines Table 15 lists the checkpoints and the training data that each baseline reports, and Appendix gives the tool and the settings of each model. Open base models. Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B are the open vision-language models from which ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B are trained. Without tool, they answer from the first view. With zoom tool (+ tool), they show what the base model reaches before it is trained with CrossRPO. ZwZ2-9B and ZwZ2-27B [71] are trained from Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B to read fine details and to connect several pieces of evidence in the whole image, without zoom tool. We run them without tool and with the zoom tool. 53 Vision-OPD-9B [81] is trained from Qwen3.5-9B by on-policy self-distillation to see fine details without tool. With the zoom tool, it zooms on 4.3% of the ViRA-Bench images at 1 MP  (Table 23)  . Released zoom agents (79B). These agents are based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B [3] and use their own tools and prompts. DeepEyes [87] is trained with RL to call zoom tool that crops box of the image, and tool call adds to its reward. DeepEyesV2 [25] extends DeepEyes to an agent that writes and runs code on the image. Mini-o3 [33] is trained for visual search over many turns, and we allow the 32 turns of its own evaluation. Thyme [85] writes code that crops, rotates or enhances the image and runs it in sandbox. Pixel Reasoner [59] is trained with curiosity reward to use pixel-space operations such as zooming into region. ZoomEye [57] requires no training. It searches tree of crops with Qwen2.5-VL-7B in our runs and answers from the crop it selects or from the whole image. Released zoom agents (2732B). LBS-27B [78] is trained from Qwen3.8-27B. It transfers training on GUI grounding to visual observation and crops region with text action, up to three times. SenseNova-MARS-32B [9] is trained with RL to reason with crop tool and two search tools. We run it offline, so its searches return no results. Proprietary models. Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna are proprietary models that we query through their APIs. They call our zoom tool by function calling and run at three thinking levels. Their largest inputs are 3.8 MP and 30.7 MP. Baseline settings in Figure 2. The counts below each set in Figure 2 are over 15 baseline settings at 1 MP: Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna at their highest and medium thinking levels (four settings), the five open base models with the zoom tool (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B, ZwZ2-9B, ZwZ2-27B and Vision-OPD-9B), and the six released 79B agents (DeepEyes, DeepEyesV2, Mini-o3, Thyme, Pixel Reasoner and ZoomEye). setting is counted if it gives the originals answer to all three versions of the set. D.2 Benchmarks Contrast-set benchmarks. The metric is set accuracy. ViRA-Bench (Section 4) has 762 contrast sets on 466 photos of 24 to 108 MP. Each set has an original and two edited variants with different answers. ViRA-Bench-Real (Appendix B.3) has 78 contrast sets that were photographed without editing. General benchmarks. Each question is about single image, and the metric is accuracy. [73] has 191 multiple-choice questions about the attributes and the relative positions of small objects in high-resolution photos. It tests visual search. HR-Bench [66] has 800 questions on 4K images and 800 on 8K images. They ask about one small object or about the relation between several objects. 54 MME-RealWorld-Lite [84] has 1,919 multiple-choice questions from MME-RealWorld. Its tasks cover perception and reasoning on high-resolution images from five domains (text in the wild, remote sensing, diagrams and tables, monitoring, and autonomous driving). TreeBench [65] has 405 multiple-choice questions on dense photos, in which the target covers about 3% of the image on average. It tests perception and reasoning that depend on small region. O3-Bench [36] has 345 questions on large charts and maps with median of 19 MP. question requires finding and combining several regions. MMStar [8] has 1,500 multiple-choice questions that were selected so that they cannot be answered without the image. It tests general perception and reasoning, and most of its images are below 1 MP. HallusionBench [19] asks yes-or-no questions about images that contradict common knowledge or contain visual illusions. It tests whether model answers from the image or from its prior, and we use its 951 questions that come with an image. Text benchmarks. ConFiQA [4] pairs question about Wikidata facts with an LLM-written passage in which the answer entity is replaced, so the passage contradicts what the model remembers. We build text contrast sets from it (Section 5.4). NQ-Swap [46] and FaithEval [48] are used only for testing. NQ-Swap replaces the answer entity in Wikipedia passages of Natural Questions, and FaithEval pairs multiple-choice science questions with passages that state counterfactual facts.

G.2 Zoom-box size on ViRA-Bench-Real On ViRA-Bench-Real, the pooled RLOO ablation is ahead of ViRA-9B at every budget below the maximum resolution  (Table 3)  , although it is behind on ViRA-Bench. Its zoom behavior explains the difference. Both agents put the object inside their last zoom on about 95% of the images. However, ViRA-9B almost always zooms once, with box of about 1.1 to 1.5 MP of the photo regardless of the size of the object. In contrast, the ablation draws boxes of 0.3 to 0.7 MP and zooms again more often. At 0.5 MP, the objects longer side therefore spans median of 24 px in ViRA-9Bs last view and 32 px in the ablations. When the object has the same size in the last view, the two agents are equally accurate. On ViRA-Bench, the objects are larger (a longer side of 10 px at 1 MP instead of 6 px), so their longer side still spans median of 36 px in ViRA-9Bs last view at 0.5 MP, and the gap between the two agents disappears. To test this, we enlarged every zoom box of the ablation around its center, which keeps the object inside the box. We evaluated the result on 128 photographed sets, the 78 sets of ViRA-Bench-Real and 50 further sets shot in the same way, with three runs each. Doubling the box area lowers its set accuracy at 0.5, 1 and 2 MP from 40.4 / 52.6 / 66.7 to 33.1 / 44.5 / 58.1. This is close to ViRA-9B (30.5 / 42.4 / 53.9). Quadrupling the box area gives 18.5 / 39.8 / 56.8. Shrinking ViRA-9Bs boxes around their centers does not help, because the smaller box often cuts the object off. 63 The per-version GRPO ablation shows the same effect. It is ahead of ViRA-9B up to 4 MP on ViRABench-Real and at 0.5 and 1 MP on ViRA-Bench  (Table 3)  . This agent zooms 2.0 to 2.7 times per image, and its last box covers median of 0.05 to 0.23 MP of the photo. At 0.5 MP on ViRA-BenchReal, the objects longer side spans median of 49 px in its largest view that contains the object, twice the 24 px of ViRA-9B. The additional zooms cost tokens: on ViRA-Bench it uses 27K to 233K tokens per set, against 12K to 147K for ViRA-9B  (Table 17)  . Its small boxes also miss the object more often. On ViRA-Bench, at least one of its zooms covers the object on 84.5% to 92.1% of the images, against 88.4% to 97.0% for ViRA-9B, and it is behind ViRA-9B from 2 MP on. At half the area, coverage falls from 95% to 78%. However, on the images where the smaller box still covers the object, accuracy rises from 61% to 72% at 0.5 MP. The low-budget gap on ViRA-Bench-Real is thus matter of box size rather than of reading. For the five open models, heatmap shows where the model looks in the shown image while it writes its final reply. The shown image is the last crop that the model received, or its first view of the whole photo if it received no crop. We replay the saved episode and take the attention from the tokens of the final reply to the 𝑇 tokens of this image, averaged over heads. For long reply, we use 256 evenly spaced tokens of it. We use only the layers with full attention: 8 of the 32 layers in Qwen3.5-9B and ViRA-9B, 16 of the 64 layers in LBS-27B and ViRA-27B, and all 28 layers in DeepEyesV2. As in [82], we also give the model the same image alone with the request Write general description of the image. and take the attention from the last token of this prompt to the image. In each layer, we normalize both attentions to sum to one over the 𝑇 image tokens and divide the first by the second plus 1/𝑇. The division removes image tokens that receive high attention under any request, and the term 1/𝑇 keeps the ratio bounded where the second attention is near zero. The heatmap is the mean of this ratio over the layers. We clip it at its 99th percentile, upsample and smooth it to the size of the image, and draw it with the jet colormap, with low values left transparent. The proprietary models have no heatmap, because their attention is not available. Cases. In Figures 8 and 9, baselines answer from common sense.
